tagline: Up a north-running river and around the Selkirks.
intro: Out of Newport the loop turns north beside the Pend Oreille River, which flows north toward Canada and takes the road along with it. Near Usk the Kalispel Tribe's bison may be seen grazing off LeClerc Road. Above Ione the highway crosses the river and runs up through the Colville National Forest to the border.

The loop goes around the Selkirk Mountains through British Columbia, over Kootenay Lake on a free ferry, and comes back into Idaho at Porthill. From there nearly all of it keeps to river or lakeshore, south to Bonners Ferry on the Kootenai and on to Sandpoint on Lake Pend Oreille, the largest and deepest lake in Idaho.

moments.title: Tiger
moments.text: At the junction of highways 20 and 31, a 1913 store and post office is all that is left of Tiger, and it keeps the town's museum, open in season.

moments.title: Metaline Falls
moments.text: Where the river zigzags around Washington Rock, the newspaper and most of this lead-and-zinc town vouched for their Japanese-American hardware merchant in 1942, and the FBI let him go.

moments.title: Bonners Ferry
moments.text: A gold-rush ferry crossing that once stood on stilts against the Kootenai floods, where in 1974 the Kootenai Tribe declared war, tolled the highway through town and came away with a reservation.

practical: The loop crosses the Canadian border twice. Portions of the Idaho route may close in winter, and the road can be icy.

sources.label: Washington State Tourism, International Selkirk Loop
